new_statements.quote: El acento prosódico recae en la primera sílaba de la palabra, que también lleva un tono alto. Además en la tercera sílaba recae un acento prosódico más ligero, también con tono alto. En algunas palabras del dialecto meneca, el acento recae en la segunda sílaba y está marcado. El dialecto murui es el único dialecto del huitoto, según nuestros estudios, en que el acento va regularmente en la primera sílaba.
new_statements.translation: Prosodic stress falls on the first syllable of the word, which also carries a high tone. In addition a lighter prosodic stress falls on the third syllable, also with high tone. In some words of the Meneca dialect the stress falls on the second syllable and is marked. The Murui dialect is, according to our studies, the only dialect of Huitoto in which the stress regularly goes on the first syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (Gordon: initial stress, initial stress) on primary placement and adds detail: a secondary stress on the third syllable, high tone on the stressed syllables, the absence of closed syllables, and the explicit dialect restriction (Murui only; Meneca words may have second-syllable stress).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress is on the first syllable of the word (Murui dialect), and the stressed syllable also bears high tone; a weaker secondary stress with high tone falls on the third syllable. Syllables are (C)V(VV) with no codas, so no weight distinction is at play. Tomo II (Castellano-Huitoto Murui list and the grammatical notes appendix) says nothing further about stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: a lighter prosodic stress ('acento prosódico más ligero'), also with high tone, on the third syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Words of the Meneca dialect (some entries in the dictionary belong to other Huitoto dialects and are labelled as such) can have stress on the second syllable; in those entries the stress is marked. Burtch states Murui is the only Huitoto dialect with regular initial stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Burtch 1983 describes the Murui dialect of Huitoto (Peru: Ampiyacu, Napo, Putumayo, Cara-Paraná; 1500-2000 speakers per the prologue). The dictionary also lists some entries from other Huitoto dialects (Meneca and others, labelled), and Burtch says the Meneca dialect can stress the second syllable in some words. The stress rule quoted is therefore Murui-specific and the catalog record 'Huitoto' should be read as Murui Huitoto (muru1274). The archive.org item 'huitotodiccionario' turned out to be Minor & Minor, Vocabulario Huitoto Muinane (SLP 5), a different Huitotoan variety, and was not used.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding fixed-strict initial (initial stress) rests on Wojtylak 2017 §2.2, a 613-pp modern reference grammar (JCU PhD, published Brill 2020) that we hold as PDF+text; the deciding sentences are verbatim at pp. 94-96 and say primary stress is word-initial and non-contrastive, with secondary stress in 4+-syllable words usually on the linker -dɨ/-tɨ. This is the best available description; Two open items downloaded now (Villa & Idrobo 1972 phonemic sketch of Colombian Witoto; Burtch 1983 grammar-appendix excerpt) are silent on stress position. The record's grade/quote/cite top-level fields are blank although the sources entry carries the verified quotation, so the only action is to fill the strength of the evidence (primary reference grammar, quote verified)

No statement of stress position.
